description: The Trinity, Nicene Creed, Catholic creation belief and the dignity of the human person.
content_html:
One God, Three Persons

At the heart of Catholic Christianity is the belief that God is the Trinity — one God who exists as three co-equal and co-eternal persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. This is not a belief in three separate gods. Catholic teaching insists firmly on the oneness of God alongside the three-ness of persons. The technical phrase that earns marks in your exam is “one God, three persons” or, in the language of the early Church, una substantia, tres personae — one substance, three persons. Each person is distinct but not separate.

Key Fact

The Trinity: God the Father is the creator and sustainer of all things; God the Son (Jesus Christ) is the incarnate Word who redeems humanity; God the Holy Spirit is the presence of God active in the world and in believers today. One God, three persons — this is the foundational Catholic belief.

Scriptural Roots of the Trinity

The doctrine of the Trinity is rooted in scripture. At the baptism of Jesus, all three persons appear together: Jesus is baptised, the Holy Spirit descends “like a dove”, and the voice of the Father speaks: “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:13–17). The Gospel of John deepens the Trinitarian picture: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). This Logos became flesh in Jesus (John 1:14).

The Nicene Creed and Councils

The Nicene Creed is recited at every Catholic Mass as the authoritative summary of the faith. It declares “We believe in one God” before naming each person of the Trinity in turn. The Creed was produced at two councils: the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE), which condemned the heresy that Jesus was a lesser created being, and the First Council of Constantinople (381 CE), which settled the status of the Holy Spirit. The key Greek term agreed at Nicaea is homoousios — meaning “of the same substance” as the Father — affirming that the Son is fully God, not a demigod.

Homoousios means “of the same substance” — not “the same person.” The Arian heresy (condemned at Nicaea) held that the Son was a lesser, created being (homoiousios — similar substance). The Nicene settlement was precise: the Son shares the same divine nature as the Father, but the Father and Son remain distinct persons. This distinction is crucial for the Trinitarian doctrine — students who write “the Son is the Father” are falling into a different ancient heresy called Modalism.

Creation and Genesis

The Bible opens with two complementary accounts of creation in Genesis 1–3. Catholic teaching does not require these to be read as science. Instead, the Church understands them as theological accounts revealing truths about God and human beings. Genesis 1 is a majestic, structured poem: God creates in six days and rests on the seventh. Each stage is declared “good”, and the whole declared “very good” (Genesis 1:31). Genesis 2 is a more intimate narrative about humanity’s formation and relationship with God.

Key Fact

Genesis 1:27 declares: “God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.” The phrase imago Dei (Latin: “image of God”) is central to Catholic teaching on human dignity: every human being possesses inherent worth that cannot be taken away, regardless of ability, status or actions.

Image of God, Dominion and Stewardship

Being made in the imago Dei has two practical implications for Catholics. First, every human life must be respected — from conception to natural death — because to attack a human being is to attack someone who bears God’s image. Second, Genesis 1:28 gives humanity dominion over creation. Catholic teaching distinguishes dominion from exploitation: true dominion is exercised as stewardship — caring for the earth as God’s creation rather than using it carelessly. Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015) connects stewardship directly to Catholic Social Teaching about care for creation.

Both Catholic and Protestant Christians accept Genesis 1–2 as scripture. Key differences:

  • Interpretation: Most mainstream Protestant denominations (Anglican, Methodist, Baptist) also read Genesis as theological rather than scientific. However, some evangelical and conservative Protestant groups hold to a literal six-day creation view, which the Catholic Magisterium does not require.
  • Authority to interpret: Catholics believe the Magisterium (the Church’s official teaching body) guides the correct interpretation of scripture. Most Protestant traditions rely on individual reading guided by the Holy Spirit (scripture alone — sola scriptura).
  • Original sin and creation: Both affirm the Fall (Genesis 3) as the entry of sin into creation. The Catholic view of original sin is shaped by Augustine and the Council of Trent; some Reformed Protestant traditions emphasise total depravity more strongly than Catholic theology does.
exam_tip_html: For “Outline three…” questions on the Trinity, give three distinct points — not three sentences elaborating the same idea. For example: (1) God is one substance in three persons; (2) the doctrine was defined at the First Council of Nicaea in 325 CE; (3) the Nicene Creed uses the term homoousios to affirm the Son is fully God. For the 5-mark question requiring a source of wisdom, name a specific reference such as “Matthew 3:13–17 (the baptism of Jesus, where all three persons appear)” or “John 1:1 (‘the Word was God’)” — a vague “the Bible says God is Trinity” does not earn the fifth mark. For 12-mark Discuss answers, the strongest responses cite named sources on both sides and reach a justified conclusion rather than restating the same points. SPaG marks reward precision with technical vocabulary like homoousios, imago Dei and “Nicene Creed” spelt correctly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Trinity is the foundational Catholic doctrine: one God in three co-equal, co-eternal persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), defined using the term homoousios (“same substance”) at the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and the First Council of Constantinople (381 CE).
  • Genesis 1:27 teaches that all human beings are made in the imago Dei (image of God), giving every person inherent dignity; this is the basis for Catholic teaching on the sanctity of human life and social justice.
  • Catholic teaching distinguishes dominion (Genesis 1:28) from exploitation: humanity is called to act as steward of creation, not its owner — a principle developed in modern Catholic Social Teaching on care for the environment.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Catholic beliefs about the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point. Acceptable points include:
• God is one being in three co-equal, co-eternal persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
• The doctrine was defined at the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE).
• The Nicene Creed affirms the Son is homoousios (of the same substance) as the Father.
• The Trinity is seen in the baptism of Jesus, where all three persons are present (Matthew 3:13–17).
• The Holy Spirit was confirmed as fully God at the First Council of Constantinople (381 CE).
[Maximum 3 marks — first three discrete points credited only]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Catholics believe about the creation of human beings.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per developed point. Acceptable points include:
• Catholics believe humans were created by God in the image of God (imago Dei) — Genesis 1:27.
• Being made in God's image means every human has inherent dignity that cannot be taken away.
• Genesis 2 describes God forming a human from the earth and breathing life into them, signifying both material and spiritual dimensions.
• Humanity is given dominion over creation (Genesis 1:28) but Catholics understand this as stewardship, not exploitation.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways the Nicene Creed is important for Catholic Christians.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per developed explanation.
• The Nicene Creed is recited at every Catholic Mass, uniting the global Church in a shared statement of faith — it connects Catholics to over 1,600 years of tradition and affirms the key Trinitarian beliefs settled by the early Church councils.
• The Creed uses the technical term homoousios to define the Son as being of the same substance as the Father, protecting the Church from the Arian heresy and making the doctrine of the Trinity precise and stable across denominations and centuries.
[4 marks — 2 per explanation: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic beliefs about human dignity, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per explanation plus one additional mark for a named source.
• Every human being is made in the image of God (imago Dei) — this means human life has unconditional worth regardless of ability or social status. Source: Genesis 1:27 — 'God created mankind in his own image.'
• Catholics believe that because all people bear the image of God, attacking or degrading any human life is an offence against God himself — this grounds Catholic opposition to abortion and euthanasia.
• The fifth mark requires a named, identifiable source: a Bible book and chapter:verse, or a named Catechism paragraph, or a named Church document. Vague references ('the Bible says humans are important') do not earn the fifth mark.
[5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in the Trinity is the most important Catholic Christian belief.'
Discuss this statement, giving arguments for and against, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): Both sides are fully developed with named sources; the response weighs perspectives explicitly and reaches a justified conclusion that picks a clear position. E.g. argues Trinity is foundational because all other doctrines (Incarnation, salvation, sacraments) depend on it; counter-argument could be that imago Dei or the resurrection is equally central because they more directly affect how Catholics live and treat others; conclusion weighs which teaching has the most practical and doctrinal significance.
Secure (7–9): Both sides present with some development; at least one named source (e.g. Nicene Creed, Matthew 3, Genesis 1:27); conclusion present but may be thin.
Developing (4–6): One side more developed; sources vague or absent; conclusion is descriptive rather than evaluative.
Emerging (1–3): One-sided or very brief; no sources; no genuine evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Catholic teaching about stewardship of creation influences how Catholics behave.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per developed explanation.
• Catholics believe humans are stewards, not owners, of creation (Genesis 1:28) — this leads some Catholics to support environmental campaigns, reduce consumption, and campaign against pollution, seeing it as a religious duty to care for God's creation.
• Pope Francis's teaching in Laudato Si' (2015) links stewardship to Catholic Social Teaching — Catholics are called to take the 'preferential option for the poor' in environmental issues, since the most vulnerable communities suffer most from environmental damage.
[4 marks — 2 per explanation]

knowledge_checks.q: Which term, agreed at the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE), affirms that the Son is of the same substance as the Father?
Which of the following CORRECTLY states the Catholic teaching on creation and science?
options: The Catholic Church requires Genesis 1–2 to be read as a literal scientific account.
The Catholic Church treats Genesis 1–2 as theological accounts, not scientific textbooks.
Catholics believe the world was created in exactly six 24-hour days.
The Catholic Church rejects all scientific accounts of the universe's origins.

knowledge_checks.q: The Latin phrase _____ means 'in the image of God' and describes the special dignity of every human being in Catholic teaching.
The Nicene Creed was first produced at the First Council of _____ in 325 CE.
Match each term to its correct meaning:
right: One God existing as three co-equal, co-eternal persons
Of the same substance — affirming the Son is fully God
Responsible care of creation on behalf of God

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Catholic doctrine of the Trinity state?
flashcard_questions.a: One God exists as three co-equal, co-eternal persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the term homoousios, and why did it matter at Nicaea (325 CE)?
flashcard_questions.a: It means 'of the same substance' — it affirmed the Son is fully God, not a lesser created being.

flashcard_questions.q: At which two councils was the Nicene Creed finalised?
flashcard_questions.a: First Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and First Council of Constantinople (381 CE).

flashcard_questions.q: Which passage shows all three persons of the Trinity appearing at the same moment?
What does John 1:1 teach about the Son in relation to God?
flashcard_questions.a: That the Word (Logos) 'was with God, and was God' before becoming flesh.

flashcard_questions.q: What Latin phrase describes the special dignity of every human being in Genesis 1:27?
Genesis 1:27 says God created mankind — what does it say about how?
flashcard_questions.a: In his own image — male and female he created them.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinction does Catholic teaching make between dominion and stewardship?
flashcard_questions.a: Dominion is authority over creation; stewardship means caring for it responsibly as God's caretaker.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Genesis verse gives humanity dominion over creation?
What heresy was condemned at the First Council of Nicaea?
flashcard_questions.a: Arianism — the belief that the Son was a lesser, created being.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Nicene Creed, and when is it used in Catholic worship?
flashcard_questions.a: A statement of faith formulated in 325/381 CE, recited at every Catholic Mass.

flashcard_questions.q: What does imago Dei mean for Catholic teaching on how humans should be treated?
flashcard_questions.a: Every human life has inherent dignity that cannot be taken away, regardless of ability or status.

glossary_terms.definition: The Christian doctrine that there is one God who exists as three distinct, co-equal and co-eternal persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
The first person of the Trinity; creator and sustainer of all things, to whom Jesus prays as Father.
The second person of the Trinity; the eternal Word who became human in Jesus of Nazareth.
The third person of the Trinity; God active and present in the world and in the lives of believers.
A statement of Christian belief formulated at the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and expanded at the First Council of Constantinople (381 CE), recited at every Catholic Mass.
The divine reason or Word (from Greek logos) identified in John 1 with the pre-existent Son of God, through whom all things were made.
Latin phrase meaning 'in the image of God'; describes the special dignity of every human being in Catholic teaching (Genesis 1:27).
In Genesis 1:28, the God-given authority of human beings over the rest of creation; in Catholic teaching, this carries responsibility to care for creation, not exploit it.
The responsible care and management of creation on behalf of God; humanity acts as God's caretaker, not owner, of the earth.
